title: Non-identical Bernoulli Observations
text: What happens when observations remain independent but their success probabilities change? The instructor basketball example models fatigue by moving from \(p_1=0.90\) to \(p_n=0.50\).

title: Non-identical Bernoulli Observations
text: What happens when observations remain independent but their success probabilities change? The instructor basketball example models fatigue by moving from \(p_1=0.90\) to \(p_n=0.50\).

title: Non-identical Bernoulli Observations
text:
2. Theory before simulation
Each \(X_i\) is Bernoulli, but the total is Poisson-binomial rather than ordinary Binomial. For the average,
\[
E(\bar X)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_i p_i=0.70.
\]
\[
SE(\bar X)=\frac{\sqrt{\sum_i p_i(1-p_i)}}{n}.
\]
The introductory iid CLT does not apply literally. A bounded independent-array CLT can apply because no one observation dominates the growing total variance. This is the finite bounded-variable form of the Lindeberg-Feller triangular-array argument.

title: Non-identical Bernoulli Observations
text:
3. Prediction
I expected a useful Normal shape well before the highly skewed small-Binomial case. The changing path should be slightly narrower than fixed Bernoulli 0.70 because heterogeneity reduces \(\sum p_i(1-p_i)\) when the average probability is held fixed.

title: Non-identical Bernoulli Observations
text:
4. Probability path and design


Show R code
plot_probability_paths(paths, 20)








Figure 1: Across 20 ordered shots, the changing model falls from 0.90 to 0.50 while the matched iid comparator stays at 0.70. Both have average probability 0.70.





Every evaluated \(n\) uses an evenly spaced path with the same endpoints, 10,000 repeated games, and seed 631. The primary statistic is the average; multiplying it by \(n\) gives the total number made.

title: Non-identical Bernoulli Observations
text:
8. Decision and disagreement
Decision: \(n=50\) is a practical transition point. Skewness is inside the guidance and remains small at 75 and 100, the center and SE match exact theory, and the global histogram is useful. Q-Q RMSE remains above the exact-Normal calibration because the average still lives on a lattice. That disagreement is retained rather than forcing a numerical pass.

title: Non-identical Bernoulli Observations
text:
9. Limitation and surprise
Independence is assumed, not observed. In a real game, confidence, defense, and earlier outcomes could create dependence. The useful surprise is that changing probabilities do not automatically make the approximation worse: with the same average probability, this path is slightly less variable than fixed Bernoulli 0.70.

title: Non-identical Bernoulli Observations
text:
10. Conclusion
Identical distribution is not required for every Normal approximation. Here bounded independent observations, a growing total variance, and a vanishing largest variance share support a generalized CLT, with a practical transition near 50 observations.

title: Creative Case: Heritage-Language Retention
text:
ImportantCreative simplified simulation



This page is not observed cultural data and is not a validated sociological model. It does not describe or rank any named language or community. Retention and shift are not treated as inherently better or worse.

title: Creative Case: Heritage-Language Retention
text:
1. Question and role
How does an average behave when stylized retention probabilities vary across ordered household or contextual positions? The purpose is mathematical: to compare equal-mean Bernoulli paths, not to explain real cultural transmission.

title: Creative Case: Heritage-Language Retention
Creative Case: Heritage-Language Retention
text:
3. Exact order invariance
The increasing and decreasing paths contain the same probabilities in reverse order. Under independence, the distribution of their total is therefore exactly the same. Order can change the story attached to a sequence, but it cannot change this Poisson-binomial distribution.


Show R code
plot_probability_paths(paths, 50)








Figure 1: The neutral gallery holds average probability at 0.60 while varying heterogeneity and direction. Increasing and decreasing paths are reversals, not competing cultural narratives.

title: Creative Case: Heritage-Language Retention
text:
4. Prediction and design
I expected the increasing and decreasing paths to agree up to Monte Carlo noise. The changing paths should be slightly narrower than the stable path because spreading probabilities around the same mean lowers the sum of Bernoulli variances.
Static results use seed 631, 10,000 repetitions, and sample sizes from 10 through 200. The browser tool later on is supplemental and uses 3,000 deterministic repetitions for responsiveness.

8. Decision and disagreement
For this stylized whole-distribution comparison, \(n=50\) is practically useful. The histograms are globally bell-shaped, skewness is modest, and the result remains stable at 75 and 100. Q-Q RMSE remains above the continuous calibration because of the Bernoulli lattice.

title: Creative Case: Heritage-Language Retention
text:
9. Limitation
The model cannot explain real retention, shift, identity, or community change. Its probabilities are chosen for a mathematical comparison, not measured. Dependence, social networks, varying definitions, and unequal contexts would all matter in a real study.

title: Creative Case: Heritage-Language Retention
text:
10. Conclusion
Changing probabilities alter variance even when the average probability is held fixed. Reversing the same probability set does not alter the distribution under independence, which separates the mathematics of order from any real-world narrative.

title: Synthetic Age-at-Death Mixture
text:
WarningSynthetic distribution



This graph-inspired population is not fitted historical mortality data. It is used only to study how averaging acts on a bounded, irregular, two-component distribution.

title: Synthetic Age-at-Death Mixture
text:
1. Question and role
How quickly does an average become approximately Normal when the parent distribution has a sharp early component, a broad later component, and a deep valley between them?

title: Synthetic Age-at-Death Mixture
text:
2. Population construction
For integer support from 0 through 100, the instructor construction uses
\[
w_E(x)=0.045e^{-x/5}.
\]
\[
w_A(x)=0.030\exp\left[-\frac12\left(\frac{x-65}{10}\right)^2\right].
\]
then normalizes \(w_E(x)+w_A(x)\) to sum to one.


Show R code
plot_age_components(population$distribution)








Figure 1: The synthetic population combines a rapidly decreasing early component with a broad component centered near 65. The normalized curve is a mathematical construction, not an empirical life table.

title: Synthetic Age-at-Death Mixture
text:
3. Theory and prediction
Exact weighted sums give mean 49.98 and SD 27.63. The observations are iid, bounded, and finite-variance, so the ordinary CLT applies. I expected the bimodal parent to leave visible asymmetry at small \(n\), then converge faster than the unbounded Exponential case.

title: Synthetic Age-at-Death Mixture
text:
4. Simulation design
The grid runs from \(n=1\) through 300 with extra attention near 75. Every point uses 10,000 repeated samples and seed 631. The same calibrated evidence categories used for the required populations are retained.

8. Decision and disagreement
Decision: \(n=75\) is the smallest defensible tested value. Skewness is about -0.073, the histogram and Q-Q plot are convincing, and the conclusion remains visually stable at 100 and 150. Q-Q RMSE moves just above the calibration band at some larger points; that small fluctuation is retained as Monte Carlo disagreement rather than interpreted as reversed convergence.

title: Synthetic Age-at-Death Mixture
text:
9. Limitation and surprise
The numerical result belongs only to this constructed probability vector. It says nothing about any population, place, or historical period. The surprise is how completely averaging can conceal a parent with two visibly separate components.

title: Synthetic Age-at-Death Mixture
text:
10. Conclusion
A bounded but highly irregular parent can yield a useful Normal approximation by about 75 observations. Parent multimodality alone does not prevent the ordinary CLT.

title: Exponential
text: The Exponential parent is continuous but strongly right-skewed. I expected the ordinary CLT to work, yet much more slowly than for the symmetric die because averaging must tame a long right tail.

title: Exponential
text: The Exponential parent is continuous but strongly right-skewed. I expected the ordinary CLT to work, yet much more slowly than for the symmetric die because averaging must tame a long right tail.

title: Exponential
text:
2. Parent population


Show R code

Figure 1: The rate-1 Exponential density concentrates near zero and extends to the right. This asymmetry is the feature averaging must overcome.

title: Exponential
text:
3. Theory before simulation
For \(X_i \sim Exp(1)\), \(E(X)=1\) and \(Var(X)=1\). All ordinary CLT conditions hold, giving center 1 and theoretical standard error \(1/\sqrt{n}\).
The exact sample sum is Gamma, so the remaining standardized skewness shrinks like \(2/\sqrt{n}\). This predicts slow but steady progress.

title: Exponential
text:
9. Decision and disagreement
Decision: use \(n=1000\) as the conservative threshold. The region from 750 to 1000 is where the practical shape becomes credible, but \(n=300\) and 500 are seed-sensitive. At 1000, skewness and Q-Q RMSE are inside the guidance bands for both seeds, the dark Normal overlay and Q-Q line agree closely, and the primary-seed conclusion persists at \(n=1500\) and 2000. Q-Q fluctuation at seed 1631 and \(n=1500\) remains visible rather than being hidden.

title: Exponential
text:
10. Limitation and surprise
A single threshold cannot serve every tail probability. The most useful surprise is how early the mean and SE look correct compared with the shape: first and second moments alone would have declared victory much too soon.

title: Standard Cauchy
text: Can a huge sample rescue an average from a standard Cauchy parent? No. The population has no finite mean or variance, so the ordinary CLT does not apply. I predicted persistent heavy tails at every \(n\).

title: Standard Cauchy
text: Can a huge sample rescue an average from a standard Cauchy parent? No. The population has no finite mean or variance, so the ordinary CLT does not apply. I predicted persistent heavy tails at every \(n\).

title: Standard Cauchy
text:
2. Parent population


Show R code
plot_parent_population(population)








Figure 1: The central standard-Cauchy density resembles a bell, but its tails decay too slowly for a finite mean or variance. Central appearance alone is therefore deceptive.

title: Standard Cauchy
text:
3. Theory before simulation
If \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) are independent standard Cauchy variables, then
\[
\frac{X_1+\cdots+X_n}{n} \sim Cauchy(0,1).
\]
The sample mean has exactly the same distribution for every \(n\). Population mean, variance, and theoretical SE are unavailable, so reporting them would be mathematically false.

title: Standard Cauchy
text:
4. Simulation design
I simulated 10,000 means at each of \(n=1,2,5,10,30,100,500,\) and 1000 with seed 631. All observations, including extremes, enter the quantiles and maximum. Histograms show only the declared central window \([-10,10]\) and report the omitted fraction.

title: Standard Cauchy
text:
7. Why ordinary diagnostics are absent
Sample SD, moment skewness, and moment kurtosis exist for a finite simulated batch, but they are dominated by whichever rare extreme appears. They do not estimate stable Cauchy population moments. I therefore mark center, theoretical SE, relative SE error, skewness, excess kurtosis, and Normal Q-Q RMSE unavailable rather than presenting unstable numbers as comparable evidence.

title: Standard Cauchy
text:
8. Robust comparison
For a standard Cauchy, the theoretical 1st and 99th percentiles are approximately -31.82 and 31.82, and the IQR is exactly 2. The simulated values in the table remain close across \(n\), even while the maximum varies wildly. Robust center and spread tell the stable story better than sample variance.

title: Standard Cauchy
text:
9. Decision
Decision: no ordinary-CLT threshold exists. The failure is theoretical and empirical. Larger samples do not narrow the distribution of the mean, and persistent extreme means are part of the result rather than data errors.

title: Standard Cauchy
text:
10. Limitation and surprise
Any finite simulation understates some possible tail events, and a central plot cannot display an unbounded range. The striking surprise is that averaging 1,000 observations changes neither the law nor the typical IQR of the mean. More data do not repair a missing first moment.

title: How Fast Does Normal Happen?
text:
Five parent populations enter. Their sample means do not all approach the bell curve at the same pace, and one never does.
This project uses repeated sampling to ask a practical version of the Central Limit Theorem: how large must the sample be before a Normal approximation is genuinely useful? Each analysis begins with a prediction, checks the theorem, and then compares graphical and numerical evidence.

title: How Fast Does Normal Happen?
text:
Research question

How does the population distribution affect the sample size required for the sampling distribution of the mean to become approximately Normal?

The broader question is when an average is trustworthy and when population shape or failed assumptions make it misleading.

title: How Fast Does Normal Happen?
text:
Population versus sampling distribution
The population distribution describes individual observations, such as one die roll or one Exponential waiting time. The sampling distribution of the mean describes the averages produced by repeatedly drawing an entire sample of size \(n\). This project holds the population fixed within each case, repeats the sampling experiment 10,000 times, and studies the resulting 10,000 averages.

title: How Fast Does Normal Happen?
text:
The CLT in plain language
When observations are independent, identically distributed, and have a finite mean and variance, their standardized sample mean approaches a Normal shape as \(n\) grows. The theorem does not promise that \(n=30\) is always enough, and it does not apply to the Cauchy mean. Symmetry, skewness, discreteness, and tail weight determine how useful the approximation is at finite \(n\).

title: How Fast Does Normal Happen?
text:
Seven-step experimental protocol
Before examining final empirical conclusions, I used the same sequence for all five cases:

Establish the scientific question.
Build and verify a minimal reusable simulation.
Explore candidate diagnostics.
Experiment with visual forms.
Develop an operational evidence standard from the exploration.
Rerun the complete analysis consistently.
Verify, interpret, and render the final results.

title: How Fast Does Normal Happen?
text:
Answer first
The parent distribution matters enormously. Standard Normal needs no waiting: \(n=1\) is exact. A symmetric die is useful by \(n=30\). The skewed small Binomial needs about \(n=200\), and a conservative Exponential threshold is \(n=1000\) after a second seed rejects the earlier \(n=300\) impression. Standard Cauchy never reaches an ordinary-CLT threshold because its sample mean remains Cauchy at every \(n\).


Show R code
thresholds <- data.frame(
  population = factor(c("Standard Normal", "Six-sided die", "Small Binomial", "Exponential"), levels = rev(c("Standard Normal", "Six-sided die", "Small Binomial", "Exponential", "Standard Cauchy"))),
  n = c(1, 30, 200, 1000),
  color = c("#0d6973", "#3a7697", "#8b4f79", "#bd5b32")
)

title: How Fast Does Normal Happen?
text:
The five investigations

Standard Normal: an exact reference case at every sample size.
Six-sided die: bounded, discrete, and symmetric.
Exponential: continuous with a long right tail.
Small Binomial: discrete, zero-heavy, and right-skewed.
Standard Cauchy: a stress test with no finite mean or variance.

title: How Fast Does Normal Happen?
text:
What each diagnostic contributed

Center: all finite-variance cases centered correctly well before their shapes were convincing.
Standard error: the theoretical \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\) relationship worked early and did not by itself certify Normality.
Skewness: this separated the symmetric die from the two asymmetric parents.
Excess kurtosis: this exposed tail and peak differences that skewness could miss.
Q-Q RMSE: this was the strictest diagnostic, especially for discrete lattices.
Plots: these determined whether the remaining numerical departure would materially mislead a Normal approximation.

title: How Fast Does Normal Happen?
text:
Evidence standard
The final decision does not come from a single score. Center, standard error, skewness, excess kurtosis, a Q-Q discrepancy, and the plots each answer a different question. Numerical bands are calibrated against the finite simulation noise in the Normal case. A conclusion must also persist for the next two larger evaluated sample sizes.






NoteWhy n = 30 is not a law



At \(n=30\), the die is defensible, Exponential still shows substantial right-tail curvature, and the small Binomial remains skewed and visibly discrete. Sample size cannot be judged apart from the parent shape and the intended use of the approximation.

title: How Fast Does Normal Happen?
text:
Reproducibility and limits
All final results use seed 631 and 10,000 repetitions per sample size. The borderline Exponential conclusion was repeated with seed 1631; that run rejected the first impression at 300 and motivated the conservative 1000 threshold. The simulations cannot prove a universal threshold, and tail-sensitive applications may require larger samples than the practical whole-distribution judgments here.
See the methodology decisions and curated AI interaction log for the full decision trail.

title: How Fast Does Normal Happen?
text:
Beyond the iid foundation
The completed Extensions section tests assumptions rather than only parent shapes. It studies dependent machine failures, independent non-identical Bernoulli observations, a synthetic age-at-death mixture, and a respectful creative heritage-language thought experiment with a local interactive enhancement and full static fallback.
The five required conclusions above remain unchanged. The extension pages use separate statistical contracts so dependent or non-identical observations are never passed through an iid formula merely for consistency.

title: Small Binomial

3. Theory before simulation
The parent mean is \(5(0.10)=0.5\) and variance is \(5(0.10)(0.90)=0.45\). Independent identical observations are bounded, so the ordinary CLT applies and
\[
SE(\bar X_n)=\sqrt{\frac{0.45}{n}}.
\]
Discreteness does not violate the theorem, but it can remain visible in finite samples.

The grid is dense from \(n=1\) to 200, then checks 300 and 500 for stability. Every grid point uses 10,000 means and seed 631. The independent second-seed check is reserved for Exponential, the genuinely most borderline finite-variance case.

\[

The ordinary CLT applies.

title: Standard Normal
text: How quickly does Normal happen when the parent population is already Standard Normal? It happens immediately. A linear combination of independent Normal variables is Normal, so the sample mean is exactly Normal at every positive sample size. The smallest defensible answer is therefore \(n=1\).

title: Standard Normal
text: How quickly does Normal happen when the parent population is already Standard Normal? It happens immediately. A linear combination of independent Normal variables is Normal, so the sample mean is exactly Normal at every positive sample size. The smallest defensible answer is therefore \(n=1\).

title: Standard Normal
text:
2. Parent population


Show R code

title: Standard Normal
text:
3. Theory before simulation
For independent \(X_i \sim N(0,1)\),
\[
\bar X_n \sim N\left(0,\frac{1}{n}\right).
\]
The center is 0 and the standard error is \(1/\sqrt{n}\). No approximation is involved.

title: Standard Normal
text:
4. Simulation design
At every evaluated \(n\), I generated 10,000 independent sample means with seed 631. The simulated diagnostics calibrate the amount of random fluctuation expected even when Normality is exact.

title: Dependent Machine Failures
text: What changes when each operating time affects the next failure rate? This process removes independence while retaining a simple conditional Exponential model. It tests an assumption of the ordinary CLT rather than merely changing the parent shape.

title: Dependent Machine Failures
text: What changes when each operating time affects the next failure rate? This process removes independence while retaining a simple conditional Exponential model. It tests an assumption of the ordinary CLT rather than merely changing the parent shape.

title: Dependent Machine Failures
text:
2. Conditional model
The instructor model is
\[
\lambda_t=\exp\{1.25(X_{t-1}-1)\}.
\]
\[
X_t\mid X_{t-1}\sim \operatorname{Exponential}(\lambda_t).
\]
A long previous operating time raises the next rate and shortens the conditional expected time. A short previous time does the reverse.


Show R code
plot_dependent_rate_curve()








Figure 1: The conditional expected next operating time falls as the previous operating time rises. The dashed reference marks the baseline value 1, making the compensating mechanism visible.

title: Dependent Machine Failures
text:
3. Prediction before simulation
I expected alternating negative dependence: unusually long times should tend to be followed by shorter ones. That dependence may reduce the variance of an average, but it does not guarantee a rapidly Normal shape because the conditional Exponential draws remain right-skewed.

title: Dependent Machine Failures
text:
4. Experimental design
The marginal distribution has no closed form supplied by the course document. I therefore use a one-million-value reference chain after 10,000 burn-in steps to estimate its center and spread. Separately, 10,000 independent chains receive 500 burn-in steps before averages are retained through \(n=2000\).
The matched comparator resamples independently from the same estimated marginal distribution. This removes serial dependence while keeping marginal scale approximately fixed.


Show R code
plot_dependent_chain(reference_outputs$segment)








Figure 2: A short reference-chain segment alternates between longer and shorter operating times. The order matters: these observations are neither independent nor identically distributed conditional on the past.







Show R code
plot_dependent_acf(reference_outputs$acf)








Figure 3: The autocorrelation alternates in sign, beginning near -0.365 at lag 1. This compensating dependence explains why averaging can be more precise than matched independent resampling.

title: Dependent Machine Failures
text:
8. Decision and disagreement
No calibration-band threshold appears through \(n=2000\). Shape improves steadily, and the histogram becomes visually close to Normal, but skewness is still about 0.103 and Q-Q RMSE is about 0.021. Both remain outside the Normal-noise guidance.
The precision result points in the opposite direction: effective sample size is about 2778 for nominal \(n=2000\). Dependence improves precision here while delaying a conservative shape conclusion.

title: Dependent Machine Failures
text:
9. Limitation
This is one stylized Markov process, not a reliability model for a real machine. The marginal references are simulation estimates, and no general dependent-process theorem is proved here. A Normal-looking histogram would not restore the ordinary iid CLT assumptions.

title: Dependent Machine Failures
text:
10. Conclusion
Dependence changes more than standard error. In this compensating process it narrows averages, creates effective sample sizes above nominal \(n\), and still leaves detectable right-tail shape after 2,000 observations.

title: Extensions: When iid Assumptions Change
text:
The required analyses changed parent distributions while mostly preserving iid sampling. These extensions ask what happens when independence or identical distribution changes, and whether the same evidence language still makes sense.
The original five-case conclusions remain frozen. The extensions use separate simulation contracts so an ordinary iid formula is never applied merely for visual consistency.

title: Extensions: When iid Assumptions Change
text:
Four investigations

Dependent machine failures use a conditional Exponential rate determined by the previous operating time.
Non-identical Bernoulli observations preserve independence while probabilities decline from 0.90 to 0.50.
Synthetic age-at-death mixture applies the ordinary iid CLT to a bounded two-component construction.
Heritage-language creative case compares neutral equal-mean probability paths and adds one accessible interactive thought experiment.

title: Extensions: When iid Assumptions Change
text:
Central lesson
The phrase “the CLT works” is incomplete unless the theorem and process are named. The synthetic age mixture fits the ordinary iid framework. The changing Bernoulli and creative paths need a bounded independent-array argument. The machine-failure process is dependent and receives empirical, simulation-referenced comparisons rather than an invented iid SE.

title: Extensions: When iid Assumptions Change
text:
Reproducibility
All authoritative static results use seed 631 and 10,000 repetitions. The dependent case receives a seed-1631 and burn-in sensitivity check. Only compact summaries are committed. The creative browser tool is supplemental, deterministic, local, and paired with a complete static fallback.
